content: The timely identification and management of drug-resistant HIV is critical to the success of antiretroviral therapy (ART) scale-up and the broader national HIV response. Failure to address this issue promptly could undermine these efforts. Minimizing the emergence and transmission of drug-resistant HIV is a fundamental component of national HIV strategies. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes that the expansion of HIV treatment must be accompanied by robust measures to monitor and improve the quality of ART delivery and to conduct surveillance of HIV drug resistance. To this end, WHO has developed a global action plan for HIV drug resistance, which includes five strategic objectives: 1. Implement high-impact interventions to prevent and respond to the emergence of HIV drug resistance. 2. Collect high-quality data on HIV drug resistance through periodic surveys and expand routine viral load and drug resistance testing. 3. Promote relevant and innovative research to address knowledge gaps and maximize public health impact in reducing HIV drug resistance. 4. Strengthen laboratory capacity to support viral load testing and monitor HIV drug resistance, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. 5. Ensure country ownership, coordinated action, awareness, advocacy, and sustainable funding to support efforts against HIV drug resistance. WHO encourages countries to develop five-year national action plans on HIV drug resistance. These plans should align with WHO’s global and regional objectives and be integrated into national HIV strategic plans. Activities within these plans should include periodic population-level assessments of HIV drug resistance, leveraging enablers, and ensuring the timely dissemination and use of all available data. Surveillance of HIV drug resistance is essential for optimizing antiretroviral (ARV) regimens at the population level. WHO recommends that countries conduct nationally representative surveys of HIV drug resistance among various populations, including adults, children, and adolescents. These surveys provide critical data to inform the selection of first-line, second-line, and potentially third-line ART regimens. Surveillance also includes monitoring drug resistance among individuals initiating ART, those on pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and those experiencing ART failure. WHO-designated laboratories play a pivotal role in HIV drug resistance surveillance. These laboratories adhere to rigorous quality assurance processes and participate in annual proficiency testing to ensure reliable results. WHO has also established a global HIV drug resistance database, which serves as a repository for de-identified epidemiological and genomic data. Countries are encouraged to use this database to manage their HIV drug resistance data and to ensure timely interpretation and dissemination of findings at both national and global levels. Routine monitoring of quality-of-care indicators, including early warning indicators of HIV drug resistance, is recommended by WHO. These indicators help assess whether ART programs are delivering services at the quality required to minimize the emergence of drug resistance. Early warning indicators should be measured annually at the facility level and used to identify gaps in service delivery, enabling corrective actions to optimize program performance. Countries are encouraged to integrate early warning indicators into routine monitoring and evaluation systems to reduce costs and strengthen data collection processes. In settings where routine monitoring is not feasible, data can be collected from a representative sample of clinics to generalize findings at the national level. WHO also highlights the importance of timely switching to second-line ART for patients with confirmed virologic failure. This ensures effective treatment and prevents further resistance development. Additionally, monitoring ARV stock-outs at ART sites is critical to maintaining uninterrupted treatment and minimizing resistance risks. The dissemination and implementation of WHO guidelines are supported through collaboration with regional and country offices, as well as implementing partners. Countries are encouraged to analyze the resource and system requirements for guideline implementation and to engage stakeholders, including people living with HIV, in the decision-making process. This inclusive approach ensures that HIV programs are effective, equitable, and responsive to community needs. Finally, the sustainability and effectiveness of HIV programs can be enhanced by integrating them into broader health and development frameworks. Strengthening links with other health initiatives and systems is essential for long-term success.
